content: An electric toothbrush is a device designed to clean teeth using electric power to move the brush head, typically in an oscillating motion. These devices are often referred to as rotary toothbrushes due to their movement pattern. In the late 1800s, Dr. George A. Scott in the United States claimed to have invented an electric toothbrush. However, this device did not feature electronically powered bristles. Instead, it delivered a strong electrical current through the brush to the user, which was believed at the time to promote good health. The concept of a true electric toothbrush was first envisioned in 1880 and became commercially available in 1939 in Switzerland. However, it was not until 1960 that the electric toothbrush was introduced in the United States. The Broxodent, a rotating electric toothbrush, was launched by Squibb Pharmaceutical during the centennial celebration of the American Dental Association. These toothbrushes were initially developed for individuals with limited motor skills and orthodontic patients, such as those wearing braces. It has been suggested that electric toothbrushes are more effective than manual ones because they reduce the likelihood of improper brushing techniques. Over time, electric toothbrushes, such as those manufactured by Braun, have become more affordable. However, the cost of replacement brush heads remains relatively high. The electronic components of most electric toothbrushes are fully sealed to prevent water damage, and they lack metal contacts. These devices typically use inductive charging, where one half of a transformer is located in the brush unit and the other half in the charging base. When the two components are brought together, a varying magnetic field in one coil induces a current in the other, enabling the battery to charge. Some electric toothbrushes, however, use replaceable batteries, which may be disposable or rechargeable, and are usually housed in a thicker handle compared to a standard toothbrush. Independent research has shown that most electric toothbrushes are no more effective than manual toothbrushes. The exception lies in rotation-oscillation models, such as many in Braun's Oral-B series, which perform only slightly better than manual brushes. The findings emphasize that the technique of brushing is more critical to oral health than the type of toothbrush used.
